claims.source: The components of the symmetric core scaffold are long lived both in dividing yeast cells and in postmitotic cells, while several FG-Nups are turned over (D'Angelo et al., 2009; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Savas et al., 2012; Thayer et al., 2014; Toyama et al., 2013) and dynamically associate with the NPC (Dilworth et al., 2001; Niño et al., 2016; Rabut et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing FG-Nup turnover.

claims.claim: FG-Nups dynamically associate with the NPC.
claims.source: The components of the symmetric core scaffold are long lived both in dividing yeast cells and in postmitotic cells, while several FG-Nups are turned over (D'Angelo et al., 2009; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Savas et al., 2012; Thayer et al., 2014; Toyama et al., 2013) and dynamically associate with the NPC (Dilworth et al., 2001; Niño et al., 2016; Rabut et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing dynamic association of FG-Nups.

claims.claim: Previous studies in postmitotic aging cells showed changes in NPC structure and function.
claims.source: Previous studies performed in postmitotic aging cells (chronological aging) showed changes in NPC structure and function (D'Angelo et al., 2009; Toyama et al., 2019), and also in aging mitotic cells (replicative aging) changes in NPCs have been described (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Lord et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on postmitotic aging.

claims.claim: Changes in NPCs have been described in aging mitotic cells.
claims.source: Previous studies performed in postmitotic aging cells (chronological aging) showed changes in NPC structure and function (D'Angelo et al., 2009; Toyama et al., 2019), and also in aging mitotic cells (replicative aging) changes in NPCs have been described (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Lord et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on mitotic aging.

claims.claim: Individual yeast cells have a finite lifespan defined as the number of divisions they can go through before they die.
claims.source: Individual yeast cells have a finite lifespan which is defined as the number of divisions that they can go through before they die: their replicative lifespan (reviewed in Longo et al., 2012) (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast replicative aging, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The divisions in yeast are asymmetric and while the mother cell ages the daughter cell is born young.
claims.source: The divisions are asymmetric and while the mother cell ages the daughter cell is born young.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast cell division.

claims.claim: Many of the changes that characterize aging in yeast are shared with humans.
claims.source: Remarkably, studying the lifespan of this single-cell eukaryote has been paramount for our understanding of aging (reviewed in Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014; Longo et al., 2012; Nyström and Liu, 2014) and many of the changes that characterize aging in yeast are shared with humans (Janssens and Veenhoff, 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claims.claim: The cellular levels of NPC components showed loss of stoichiometry during replicative aging.
claims.source: We observe that the cellular levels of NPC components showed loss of stoichiometry during replicative aging, which were not reflected in the more stable transcriptome data (Figure 1c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteome data shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: The loss of stoichiometry in NPC components during replicative aging was not reflected in the more stable transcriptome data.
claims.source: We observe that the cellular levels of NPC components showed loss of stoichiometry during replicative aging, which were not reflected in the more stable transcriptome data (Figure 1c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of proteome and transcriptome data in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: In mitotic aging, a posttranscriptional drift of Nup levels is apparent.
claims.source: Clearly in mitotic aging, a posttranscriptional drift of Nup levels is apparent.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protein levels change while transcript levels remain stable.

claims.claim: GFP-tagged Nup133, Nup49, Nup100, Nup116 and Nup2 still localized at the nuclear envelope in old cells.
claims.source: Therefore, we validated for a subset of Nups (Nup133, Nup49, Nup100, Nup116 and Nup2) that GFP-tagged proteins expressed from their native promoters still localized at the nuclear envelope in old cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental validation using fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: Changes in relative abundance of Nup133, Nup49, Nup100, Nup116 and Nup2 at the nuclear envelope were in line with the changes found in the proteome.
claims.source: In addition, we validated that changes in relative abundance of the Nups at the nuclear envelope were in line with the changes found in the proteome.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of microscopy data with proteome data.

claims.claim: Nup116 and Nup2 showed the strongest decrease in abundance during aging.
claims.source: We included Nup116 and Nup2 in our experiments as those Nups showed the strongest decrease in abundance (Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteome data shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Nup100 is important for the permeability barrier.
claims.source: Nup100 was included because it is important for the permeability barrier (Lord et al., 2015; Popken et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Nup49 showed a relatively stable abundance profile in aging.
claims.source: The proteome data indicated that Nup49 showed a relatively stable abundance profile in aging (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteome data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: In the vast majority of aging cells the abundance of Nup116-GFP decreased relative to Nup49-mCh.
claims.source: Consistent with the proteome data, and with previously reported data (Lord et al., 2015), in the vast majority of aging cells the abundance of Nup116-GFP decreased relative to Nup49-mCh, while the abundance of Nup133-GFP appears more stable.
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1e.

claims.claim: The abundance of Nup133-GFP appears more stable during aging.
claims.source: Consistent with the proteome data, and with previously reported data (Lord et al., 2015), in the vast majority of aging cells the abundance of Nup116-GFP decreased relative to Nup49-mCh, while the abundance of Nup133-GFP appears more stable.
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1e.

claims.claim: For Nup100 and Nup2, the imaging data align well with the proteome data.
claims.source: Also for the other Nups tested (Nup100 and Nup2), the imaging data align well with the proteome data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of imaging and proteome data.

claims.claim: There is significant cell-to-cell variation in the lifespan of individual yeast cells.
claims.source: Our data contain full life histories of individual cells and, in line with previous reports (Crane et al., 2014; Fehrmann et al., 2013; Janssens and Veenhoff, 2016a; Jo et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), we observed a significant cell-to-cell variation in the lifespan of individual cells, as well as variability in the levels of fluorescent-tagged proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell life history data and citations to previous reports.

claims.claim: There is variability in the levels of fluorescent-tagged proteins in individual cells.
claims.source: Our data contain full life histories of individual cells and, in line with previous reports (Crane et al., 2014; Fehrmann et al., 2013; Janssens and Veenhoff, 2016a; Jo et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), we observed a significant cell-to-cell variation in the lifespan of individual cells, as well as variability in the levels of fluorescent-tagged proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data.

claims.claim: For Nup116 and Nup100, correlations between NPC component levels and lifespan were found, where cells with lowest levels of NE-localized GFP-tagged Nups had the shortest remaining lifespan.
claims.source: Therefore, we could assess if the changes observed for the individual NPC components correlated to the lifespan of a cell and, indeed, for Nup116 and Nup100 such correlations to lifespan were found, where those cells with lowest levels of NE-localized GFP-tagged Nups had the shortest remaining lifespan (for Nup100 r = −0.48; p=1.27×10−7 and Nup116 r = −0.56; p=6.54×10−4, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2f,g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of single-cell data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2f,g.

claims.claim: Single-cell Nup2 abundances at the NE can be highly variable.
claims.source: Single-cell Nup abundances at the NE can be highly variable (Nup2), while for other Nups (Nup100, Nup116) the loss in abundance at the NE was found in almost all aging cells and correlated with the lifespan of the cell.
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data showing variability in Nup2 levels.

claims.claim: For Nup100 and Nup116, the loss in abundance at the NE was found in almost all aging cells and correlated with the lifespan of the cell.
claims.source: Single-cell Nup abundances at the NE can be highly variable (Nup2), while for other Nups (Nup100, Nup116) the loss in abundance at the NE was found in almost all aging cells and correlated with the lifespan of the cell.
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data and correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Nup116 and Nsp1 strongly decrease in aging.
claims.source: From the joint experiments published by Janssens et al. (2015); Lord et al. (2015) and the current study we can conclude that especially Nup116 and Nsp1 (Nup98 and Nup62 in humans) strongly decrease in aging.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple studies including the current one.

claims.claim: In postmitotic cells, oxidative damage was proposed to lead to the appearance of carbonyl groups on Nups inducing more permeable NPCs.
claims.source: Indeed, in postmitotic cells, oxidative damage was proposed to lead to the appearance of carbonyl groups on Nups inducing more permeable NPCs (D'Angelo et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: NPCs remain intact during multiple divisions.
claims.source: Indeed, NPCs remain intact during multiple divisions (Colombi et al., 2013; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Khmelinskii et al., 2012; Thayer et al., 2014), and especially in aged mother cells a fraction of the NPCs is inherited asymmetrically to the aging mother cell (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In aged mother cells a fraction of the NPCs is inherited asymmetrically to the aging mother cell.
claims.source: Indeed, NPCs remain intact during multiple divisions (Colombi et al., 2013; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Khmelinskii et al., 2012; Thayer et al., 2014), and especially in aged mother cells a fraction of the NPCs is inherited asymmetrically to the aging mother cell (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Protein carbonyls can be formed through direct oxidation of Lysine, Threonine, Arginine and Proline side chains through Metal Catalyzed Oxidation.
claims.source: Here, we focused on the most prominent one, the direct oxidation of the Lysine, Threonine, Arginine and Proline (K, T, R, P) side chains through Metal Catalyzed Oxidation (MCO) (Stadtman and Levine, 2003) by the Fenton reaction (Maisonneuve et al., 2009; Stadtman and Levine, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations describing the mechanism of protein carbonylation.

claims.claim: No evidence was found for oxidative damage of Nsp1, Nup2, Nic96 and Nup133 despite extensive efforts using different in vitro and in vivo oxidative conditions and different carbonyl-detection methods.
claims.source: Despite extensive efforts and using different in vitro and in vivo oxidative conditions and using different carbonyl-detection methods we could not find evidence for oxidative damage of Nsp1, Nup2, Nic96 and Nup133 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b shows negative results for Nsp1 along with a positive control).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b.

claims.claim: There is a minor impact of carbonylation on the predicted Stokes radius of individual Nups.
claims.source: Overall, there is a minor impact of carbonylation on the predicted Stokes radius of the individual Nups and the time-averaged density of a wild type and fully oxidized NPC, with average densities around 80 mg/ml and maximum densities reaching 100 mg/ml in the center of the NPC (r < 5 nm) (Figure 2a red line, Figure 2b right panel and see Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e for individual Nups and additional models dissecting the relative impact of the change in charge and hydrophobicity upon carbonylation).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2a, 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e.

claims.claim: There is a minor impact of carbonylation on the time-averaged density of a wild type and fully oxidized NPC.
claims.source: Overall, there is a minor impact of carbonylation on the predicted Stokes radius of the individual Nups and the time-averaged density of a wild type and fully oxidized NPC, with average densities around 80 mg/ml and maximum densities reaching 100 mg/ml in the center of the NPC (r < 5 nm) (Figure 2a red line, Figure 2b right panel and see Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e for individual Nups and additional models dissecting the relative impact of the change in charge and hydrophobicity upon carbonylation).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2a, 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e.

claims.claim: Oxidative damage is unlikely to be a direct cause of altered NPC stoichiometry in replicative aging.
claims.source: We conclude that oxidative damage is unlikely to be a direct cause of altered NPC stoichiometry in replicative aging, and it is probable that the previously reported increase in permeability of NEs during chronological aging (D'Angelo et al., 2009) is actually caused by factors other than carbonylation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental and modeling data showing no evidence for oxidative damage.

claims.claim: The previously reported increase in permeability of NEs during chronological aging is probably caused by factors other than carbonylation.
claims.source: We conclude that oxidative damage is unlikely to be a direct cause of altered NPC stoichiometry in replicative aging, and it is probable that the previously reported increase in permeability of NEs during chronological aging (D'Angelo et al., 2009) is actually caused by factors other than carbonylation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the lack of evidence for carbonylation effects.

claims.claim: Mutant strains with impaired NPC assembly show that a fraction of their NPCs cluster, are covered by membranes, or cause herniations of the NE.
claims.source: In young and healthy yeast cells, phenotypes associated with misassembled NPCs are rarely seen, but mutant strains with impaired NPC assembly show that a fraction of their NPCs cluster, are covered by membranes, or cause herniations of the NE (Chadrin et al., 2010; Scarcelli et al., 2007; Webster et al., 2014; Webster et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018) (reviewed in Thaller and Patrick Lusk, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Misassembled NPCs induced by mutations are asymmetrically retained and accumulated in the mother cell over time.
claims.source: Misassembled NPCs that are induced by mutations are asymmetrically retained, and accumulated in the mother cell over time (Colombi et al., 2013; Makio et al., 2013; Webster et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The protein levels of Heh1, Rtn1 and Rtn2 are stable in abundance in aging.
claims.source: The system wide proteomics data showed that the protein levels of Heh1, Rtn1 and Rtn2 are stable in abundance in aging, while a sharp decrease in abundance was found for Vps4 (Figure 2c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c showing stable transcript levels).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: A sharp decrease in abundance was found for Vps4 in aging.
claims.source: The system wide proteomics data showed that the protein levels of Heh1, Rtn1 and Rtn2 are stable in abundance in aging, while a sharp decrease in abundance was found for Vps4 (Figure 2c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c showing stable transcript levels).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: The abundance of Heh2-GFP, Brl1-GFP and Apq12-GFP at the NE decreased relative to Nup49-mCh in aging.
claims.source: Additionally, we found that the abundance of Heh2-GFP, Brl1-GFP and Apq12-GFP at the NE decreased relative to Nup49-mCh in aging (Figure 2d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c showing stable transcript levels).
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: The levels of Heh2 and Apq12 are correlated with the remaining lifespan of the cells, where cells showing the lowest levels had the shortest remaining lifespan.
claims.source: Despite the fact that neither Heh2 nor Apq12 are essential proteins, we found their levels to be correlated with the remaining lifespan of the cells, where those cells showing the lowest levels of Heh2-GFP or Apq12-GFP had the shortest remaining lifespan (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The level of the essential protein Brl1 correlated with the remaining lifespan of the cells.
claims.source: The level of the essential protein Brl1 similarly correlated with the remaining lifespan of the cells (Figure 2f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claims.claim: The deletion of either heh2, vps4 or apq12 is sufficient to cause the appearance of misassembled NPCs in haploid cells.
claims.source: Previous work showed that the deletion of either heh2, vps4 or apq12 is sufficient to cause the appearance of misassembled NPCs in haploid cells (Scarcelli et al., 2007; Webster et al., 2014) so the decrease in abundance of the proteins Heh2, Apq12, Brl1 and Vps4 suggests that NPC assembly is compromised in aging and misassembled NPCs may accumulate.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The decrease in abundance of Heh2, Apq12, Brl1 and Vps4 suggests that NPC assembly is compromised in aging.
claims.source: Previous work showed that the deletion of either heh2, vps4 or apq12 is sufficient to cause the appearance of misassembled NPCs in haploid cells (Scarcelli et al., 2007; Webster et al., 2014) so the decrease in abundance of the proteins Heh2, Apq12, Brl1 and Vps4 suggests that NPC assembly is compromised in aging and misassembled NPCs may accumulate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the decrease in abundance of proteins known to be involved in NPC assembly.

claims.claim: Chm7 is the nuclear adaptor for the ESCRT system.
claims.source: To get a more direct readout of problems in NPC assembly. we studied Chm7, the nuclear adaptor for the ESCRT system (Gu et al., 2017; Olmos et al., 2016; Webster et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The frequency of Chm7 focus formation is related to NPC assembly problems.
claims.source: Chm7 sometimes forms a focus at the NE and the frequency of focus formation is related to NPC assembly problems as mutant strains with impaired NPC assembly show more frequently Chm7 foci at the NE (Webster et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Chm7 foci are more than twice as frequently seen in the highest age group (age 15–24) compared to cells younger than five divisions.
claims.source: Indeed, the foci are more than twice as frequently seen in the highest age group (age 15–24), compared to cells younger than five divisions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification of Chm7 foci in aged cells.

claims.claim: The frequency at which cells have more than one Chm7 focus present at the NE is more than fourfold higher in the oldest age group.
claims.source: Also, the frequency at which cells have more than one focus present at the NE is more than fourfold higher in the oldest age group (Figure 2g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: The increased frequency of Chm7 foci in aged cells supports that aged cells have problems in NPC assembly.
claims.source: The increased frequency of Chm7 foci in aged cells supports that aged cells have problems in NPC assembly.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased Chm7 foci, which are markers of NPC assembly problems.

claims.claim: In young cells NE herniations are found in only 2% of the nuclei.
claims.source: In young cells NE herniations are found in only 2% of the nuclei. In aged cells, those herniations are found much more frequently, with 17% of the nuclei showing a herniation (Figure 3a,b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification of herniations shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: In aged cells, NE herniations are found in 17% of the nuclei.
claims.source: In young cells NE herniations are found in only 2% of the nuclei. In aged cells, those herniations are found much more frequently, with 17% of the nuclei showing a herniation (Figure 3a,b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification of herniations shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Four proteins involved in the assembly of NPCs decrease strongly in abundance in aging (Vps4, Heh2, Brl1 and Apq12) in a manner that correlates with remaining lifespan.
claims.source: We conclude that four proteins involved in the assembly of NPCs decrease strongly in abundance in aging (Vps4, Heh2, Brl1 and Apq12) in a manner that correlates with remaining lifespan (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The decrease in abundance of Vps4, Heh2, Brl1, Apq12 and FG-Nups likely directly cause the NPC assembly problems observed in aged cells.
claims.source: Jointly, the decrease in abundance of those proteins, and potentially also the decrease of FG-Nup abundance (Figure 1), likely directly cause the NPC assembly problems, which we observe as an increased Chm7 focus formation frequency (Figure 2g) and an increased number of herniations (Figure 3) in aged cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between protein decreases and assembly problems.

claims.claim: Passive permeability is not altered significantly in aging.
claims.source: We measured the rate of efflux in single aging cells and find that passive permeability is not altered significantly in aging (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c), excluding the possibility that NPCs with compromised permeability barriers ('leaky' NPCs) are prevalent in aging cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of efflux rates shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c.

claims.claim: NPCs with compromised permeability barriers ('leaky' NPCs) are not prevalent in aging cells.
claims.source: We measured the rate of efflux in single aging cells and find that passive permeability is not altered significantly in aging (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c), excluding the possibility that NPCs with compromised permeability barriers ('leaky' NPCs) are prevalent in aging cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the efflux measurements.

claims.claim: The cellular abundance of Crm1, Kap60 and Kap95 is relatively stable in aging.
claims.source: The cellular abundance of Crm1, Kap60 and Kap95 is relatively stable in aging (Janssens et al., 2015) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c for transcript levels) as is their abundance at the NE and their localization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data from Janssens et al., 2015 and imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In the vast majority of cells, GFP carrying a tcNLS accumulated more strongly in the nucleus at high ages.
claims.source: In the vast majority of cells, we observed that GFP carrying a tcNLS accumulated more strongly in the nucleus at high ages (Figure 4a, middle panel), and, interestingly, the GFP carrying a NES is more strongly depleted from the nucleus in the vast majority of cells (Figure 4a, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: GFP carrying a NES is more strongly depleted from the nucleus in the vast majority of aged cells.
claims.source: In the vast majority of cells, we observed that GFP carrying a tcNLS accumulated more strongly in the nucleus at high ages (Figure 4a, middle panel), and, interestingly, the GFP carrying a NES is more strongly depleted from the nucleus in the vast majority of cells (Figure 4a, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: For the control GFP, a more stable N/C ratio is found in aging.
claims.source: For the control, GFP, we find a more stable N/C ratio in aging (Figure 4a, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Reporter proteins with Nab2NLS or Pho4NLS accumulated more strongly in the nucleus at higher ages.
claims.source: Also for these two signal sequences, we found that reporter proteins with the respective sequences accumulated more strongly in the nucleus at higher ages (Figure 4c and Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4c and 4d.

claims.claim: Deletion of apq12 increases nuclear compartmentalization of GFP-NLS and GFP-NES.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that the deletion of apq12 was sufficient to mimic the increase in compartmentalization seen in aging showing increased nuclear accumulation of GFP-NLS and exclusion of GFP-NES (Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claims.claim: Cells at a median age of two divisions in a vps4Δheh2Δ double mutant had a significantly higher N/C ratio of GFP-NLS than young cells.
claims.source: We found indeed that cells at a median age of two divisions had a significantly higher N/C ratio of GFP-NLS than young cells (Figure 3f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: The increased compartmentalization in aged cells and in the apq12 and vps4Δheh2Δ mutant can be explained if fewer functional NPCs are present in the NE.
claims.source: The increased compartmentalization in aged cells and in the apq12 and vps4Δheh2Δ mutant can be explained if fewer functional NPCs are present in the NE.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Reduced numbers of NPCs would predominantly impact passive permeability, as the rate-limiting step for NTR-facilitated-transport is not at the level of the number of NPCs but rather at the level of NTRs and cargos finding each other in the crowded cytosol with overwhelming nonspecific competition.
claims.source: Reduced numbers of NPCs would predominantly impact passive permeability, as the rate-limiting step for NTR-facilitated-transport is not at the level of the number of NPCs but rather at the level of NTRs and cargos finding each other in the crowded cytosol with overwhelming nonspecific competition (Meinema et al., 2013; Riddick and Macara, 2005; Smith et al., 2002; Timney et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Lord et al. reported a reduction in nuclear accumulation of GFP-NLS in age 6+ yeast cells isolated from a culture.
claims.source: A previous report showed a reduction in nuclear accumulation of GFP-NLS in age 6 + yeast cells isolated from a culture (Lord et al., 2015), while we see no statistically significant difference at this age.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study cited.

claims.claim: The cellular abundance of Srm1 was stable during aging.
claims.source: While the cellular abundance of Srm1 was stable during aging (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), we found that the nuclear accumulation of Srm1-GFP increased during replicative aging in most cells (Figure 4g,h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: The nuclear accumulation of Srm1-GFP increased during replicative aging in most cells.
claims.source: While the cellular abundance of Srm1 was stable during aging (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), we found that the nuclear accumulation of Srm1-GFP increased during replicative aging in most cells (Figure 4g,h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by single-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4g,h.

claims.claim: The human homologue of Srm1, Rcc1, was previously reported to have an increased nuclear concentration in myonuclei and brain nuclei of aged mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, the human homologue of Srm1, Rcc1, was previously also reported to have an increased nuclear concentration in myonuclei and brain nuclei of aged mice (Cutler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Msn2 is a transcriptional regulator that responds to various stresses and translocates to the nucleus in pulses.
claims.source: Additionally, we studied Msn2, a transcriptional regulator that responds to various stresses and translocates to the nucleus in pulses, a so-called frequency modulated transcription factor.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Msn2 function.

claims.claim: Msn2 communicates information about the environment by modifying the frequency of pulses.
claims.source: Msn2 communicates information about the environment by modifying the frequency of pulses (Figure 5a) (Cai et al., 2008; Hao and O'Shea, 2011; Hao et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Msn2 pulse dynamics are primarily determined by the rates of nuclear import and nuclear export.
claims.source: These pulse dynamics are primarily determined by the rates of nuclear import and nuclear export (Hao et al., 2013), but retention mechanisms also apply.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The average pulse widths for Msn2 in each cell increased consistently from middle-age onwards.
claims.source: We observed that, as predicted by the alterations in NPCs, the average pulse widths for each cell increased consistently from middle-age onwards (Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: Aging results in both broader and lower Msn2 pulses.
claims.source: Similarly, by aligning all Msn2 pulses on top of each other for a given age, we determined a mean pulse shape for each age (Figure 5e). These show similar characteristics, where the aging results in both broader and lower Msn2 pulses.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claims.claim: Both the pulse width and pulse prominence of Msn2 are correlated to the remaining lifespan of the cell.
claims.source: As could be expected given the striking age-related changes, both the pulse width and pulse prominence are correlated to the remaining lifespan of the cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b, r = −0.36, p<0.0001 and r = 0.47, p<0.0001 for pulse prominence and pulse width, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claims.claim: The decrease in Msn2 dynamics is likely a readout for the NPC's ability to facilitate rapid responses.
claims.source: We consider it likely, that the decrease in Msn2 dynamics is a readout for the NPC's ability to facilitate rapid responses.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Aging cells may respond more slowly to changes in their environment due to reduced nuclear cytoplasmic transport and communication.
claims.source: Aging cells may thus respond more slowly to changes in their environment due to reduced nuclear cytoplasmic transport and communication.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed changes in Msn2 dynamics.

claims.claim: The data is consistent with a model where NPC assembly and quality control are compromised in mitotic aging.
claims.source: Overall, our data is consistent with a model where NPC assembly and quality control are compromised in mitotic aging (Figure 2) and where misassembled NPCs, which specifically lack the FG-Nups that we see declining in aging (Figure 1), accumulate in aged cells (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Misassembled NPCs that accumulate in aged cells specifically lack the FG-Nups that decline in aging.
claims.source: Overall, our data is consistent with a model where NPC assembly and quality control are compromised in mitotic aging (Figure 2) and where misassembled NPCs, which specifically lack the FG-Nups that we see declining in aging (Figure 1), accumulate in aged cells (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of declining FG-Nups and accumulation of misassembled NPCs.

claims.claim: Without intervention, the loss of FG-Nups at the NE would almost certainly create leaky NPCs.
claims.source: Without intervention, the loss of FG-Nups at the NE would almost certainly create leaky NPCs (Popken et al., 2015; Strawn et al., 2004; Timney et al., 2016), as also predicted by our models of aged NPCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and modeling results.

claims.claim: Based on transport data, a scenario where leaky NPCs are present at the NE of mitotically aged cells can be excluded.
claims.source: However, based on our transport data, we can exclude a scenario where leaky NPCs are present at the NE of mitotically aged cells (Figures 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from transport measurements.

claims.claim: The data supports that misassembled NPCs get covered with membrane.
claims.source: Instead, our data supports that the misassembled NPCs get covered with membrane (Figure 3), a structure known to be present in nup116, vps4pom152 and apq12 mutant strains (Scarcelli et al., 2007; Webster et al., 2014; Webster et al., 2016; Wente and Blobel, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 3 and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Membrane-covered misassembled NPCs would prevent loss of compartmentalization but cause an overall reduction of permeable NPCs.
claims.source: This would prevent loss of compartmentalization but cause an overall reduction of permeable NPCs, which is consistent with the observed decrease in transport dynamics across the NE and the increased steady state compartmentalization (Figures 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation consistent with the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Consequential to declining quality control of NPC assembly, aged nuclei have fewer functional NPCs and significant amounts of dysfunctional NPCs that do not contribute to the overall transport kinetics.
claims.source: Altogether we propose that consequential to declining quality control of NPC assembly, aged nuclei have fewer functional NPCs and significant amounts of dysfunctional NPCs that do not contribute to the overall transport kinetics (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: An imbalance affecting the protein biogenesis machinery is the major driving force in yeast replicative aging.
claims.source: In a previous study, we generated directional networks to predict how the different changes observed in aging may be interdependent, and proposed that an imbalance affecting the protein biogenesis machinery is the major driving force in yeast replicative aging (Janssens et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from a previous study cited.

claims.claim: The defects in NPCs in aging may be a consequence of the imbalanced protein levels of the NPC components and assembly factors.
claims.source: The defects in NPCs in aging may thus be a consequence of the imbalanced protein levels of the NPC components and assembly factors.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of protein imbalances and NPC defects.

claims.claim: The imbalance in NPC components is not transcriptionally driven since, with few exceptions, the transcriptional changes in Nups, NTRs and assembly factors are small.
claims.source: This imbalance is not transcriptionally driven since, with few exceptions, the transcriptional changes in Nups, NTRs and assembly factors are small (Janssens et al., 2015), but is rather related to protein synthesis, folding and assembly.
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data from Janssens et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The imbalance in NPC components is related to protein synthesis, folding and assembly.
claims.source: This imbalance is not transcriptionally driven since, with few exceptions, the transcriptional changes in Nups, NTRs and assembly factors are small (Janssens et al., 2015), but is rather related to protein synthesis, folding and assembly.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcriptional changes despite protein level changes.

claims.claim: Nup116, Nsp1, Nup159, Nic96, Nup82, Nup157 and Nup2 appear in the middle clusters of the proteome network meaning that they are predicted to be consequential to earlier changes, but also that they drive later changes.
claims.source: Indeed, the proteome changes in the Nups are well linked to other changes in the proteome of aging cells: Nup116, Nsp1, Nup159, Nic96, Nup82, Nup157 and Nup2 appear in the middle clusters of the proteome network meaning that they are predicted to be consequential to earlier changes, but also that they drive later changes (Janssens et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by network analysis from Janssens et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The finding of correlations between remaining lifespan of a cell and the abundance of several Nups and assembly factors, as well as the transport dynamics of Msn2, supports that a potential causal relation between NPC function and lifespan may exist.
claims.source: Our finding of correlations between remaining lifespan of a cell and the abundance of several Nups and assembly factors, as well as the transport dynamics of Msn2, also supports that a potential causal relation between NPC function and lifespan may exist.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed correlations.

claims.claim: Declining NPC function will result in aberrant transcription regulation and mRNA export, and contribute to the further loss of protein homeostasis.
claims.source: Moreover, declining NPC function, which by itself is a consequence of failing protein quality control, will result in aberrant transcription regulation and mRNA export, and, with that, contributes to the further loss of protein homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the consequences of NPC decline.

claims.claim: Faulty NPCs may impact the loss of genome stability in aging.
claims.source: Lastly, faulty NPCs may impact the loss of genome stability in aging and the joint dependence of NPC assembly and genome stability on Apq12 provides an interesting observation in this context.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential consequences of faulty NPCs.

claims.claim: NPC function is a factor of importance in aging and age-related disease.
claims.source: Altogether, our study contributes to the emerging view that NPC function is a factor of importance in aging and age-related disease (Fichtman and Harel, 2014) impinging on the universal hallmarks of human aging of intercellular communication and loss of protein homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the study's findings and a citation.

claims.claim: This work provides the first clear example that the assembly of large protein complexes is a major challenge in aging of dividing cells.
claims.source: Our work also provides the first clear example that the assembly of large protein complexes is a major challenge in aging of dividing cells.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claims.claim: Loss of protein complex stoichiometry is a prominent and conserved phenotype in aging.
claims.source: Indeed, there is data to support that loss of protein complex stoichiometry is a prominent and conserved phenotype in aging (Janssens et al., 2015; Ori et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The assembly and quality control of many other long-lived large protein complexes, such as the proteasome and kinetochores, are likely compromised in mitotically aging cells.
claims.source: We speculate that the assembly and quality control of many other long-lived large protein complexes, such as the proteasome and kinetochores, both becoming highly substoichiometric in aging (Janssens et al., 2015; Ori et al., 2015), are compromised in mitotically aging cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings for NPCs and data on other complexes.

results.result: The abundance of specific NPC components (particularly FG-Nups Nup116, Nsp1, Nup100, and Nup2) decreases during replicative aging at the protein level but not at the transcript level, indicating a posttranscriptional mechanism. This was validated by both proteomics and single-cell fluorescence microscopy showing loss of stoichiometry among NPC components.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C25-C29, C33-C35, C40-C41 collectively demonstrate decreased NPC component abundance through multiple complementary approaches: proteomics data (C25-C26), single-cell imaging (C28-C29, C33-C35), and validation across different Nups (C30, C40-C41). The posttranscriptional nature is supported by stable transcript levels (C26-C27). The data are internally consistent and use appropriate controls (Nup49-mCh as reference).

results.result: Cells that maintain higher levels of specific NPC components (Nup116, Nup100) and NPC assembly factors (Heh2, Apq12, Brl1) have longer remaining lifespans, and Msn2 transport dynamics correlate with lifespan, suggesting a causal relationship between NPC function and cellular longevity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C38, C56-C57, C89, C104 demonstrate statistically significant correlations between NPC component levels and remaining lifespan using single-cell life history data. The correlations are reported with appropriate statistics (Pearson r values and p-values in C38, C89). While correlations do not prove causation, the consistency across multiple NPC components and the functional readout (Msn2 dynamics) provide strong support for the relationship.

results.result: Oxidative damage through carbonylation is unlikely to be a direct cause of altered NPC stoichiometry in replicative aging, as no experimental evidence for carbonylation of Nups was found despite extensive efforts, and computational modeling predicts minimal impact of carbonylation on NPC structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are well-supported by both negative experimental results (C46) and computational modeling (C47-C48) showing minimal predicted impact. The conclusion (C49) appropriately integrates both lines of evidence. However, C50 is more speculative about chronological aging and appropriately qualified as 'probable.' The experimental approaches were rigorous (multiple oxidative conditions, detection methods) and the modeling assumptions are clearly described.

results.result: The abundance of NPC assembly factors (Vps4, Heh2, Brl1, Apq12) decreases during aging in a manner that correlates with lifespan, suggesting that compromised NPC assembly contributes to the accumulation of misassembled NPCs in aged cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55, C59, C67-C68 demonstrate decreased abundance of assembly factors through proteomics (C53-C54) and imaging (C55), with correlations to lifespan (C56-C57, C67). The inference that this causes assembly problems (C59, C68) is supported by prior work showing these deletions cause misassembled NPCs (C58). The logic connecting decreased assembly factors to assembly problems is sound, though the causal link is inferential rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: The frequency of Chm7 foci at the nuclear envelope increases more than twofold in aged cells (age 15-24 divisions), providing direct evidence for increased NPC assembly problems during aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 establish Chm7 as a marker for NPC assembly problems (C60-C61, supported by citations) and demonstrate increased frequency in aged cells (C62-C63) with appropriate quantification. The inference that this indicates assembly problems (C64) is well-justified given the established role of Chm7. Statistical significance is indicated (p≤0.01 in Figure 2g) and sample sizes are provided.

results.result: Nuclear envelope herniations, indicative of misassembled NPCs, are present in 17% of aged cell nuclei compared to only 2% in young cells, providing ultrastructural evidence for accumulation of defective NPCs during aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C65-C66 demonstrate increased herniations in aged cells through electron microscopy with clear quantification (2% vs 17%). The inference that herniations indicate misassembled NPCs (C7) is supported by prior literature (cited in C51, C96). Sample sizes are adequate (n=103 young, n=83 aged). The EM images in Figure 3a provide visual confirmation.

results.result: Passive permeability across the nuclear envelope is not significantly altered in aging cells, excluding the presence of 'leaky' NPCs with compromised permeability barriers.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70, C95 are supported by efflux measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-c. The experimental approach (poison assay with sodium azide and 2-deoxyglucose) is appropriate for measuring passive permeability. While the data show no significant change, the statistical power could be better documented. The conclusion appropriately excludes leaky NPCs as a major phenotype in aged cells.

results.result: Aged cells show increased steady-state nuclear compartmentalization, with GFP-NLS accumulating more strongly in the nucleus and GFP-NES being more depleted from the nucleus. This phenotype is recapitulated in NPC assembly mutants (apq12Δ and vps4Δheh2Δ), suggesting it results from fewer functional NPCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 demonstrate increased compartmentalization through multiple reporter proteins (GFP-NLS, GFP-NES, Nab2NLS, Pho4NLS) with appropriate controls (GFP alone, C74). The phenocopy in assembly mutants (C76-C77) strongly supports the mechanistic interpretation (C78). The data are internally consistent and use appropriate statistical tests (non-overlapping notches in box plots). The mechanistic explanation is inferential but well-reasoned.

results.result: The nuclear accumulation of Srm1-GFP increases during replicative aging despite stable cellular abundance, and this phenotype is conserved in aged mice (Rcc1, the human homologue).
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are supported by proteomics (stable abundance) and imaging data (increased nuclear accumulation) shown in Figure 4g-h. The conservation in mice (C83) is supported by citation. However, the interpretation is complicated by Srm1's retention mechanisms, which the authors acknowledge. The result is descriptive and the functional significance is unclear, but the observations are well-documented.

results.result: Msn2 transcription factor dynamics are altered in aged cells, with pulse widths increasing and pulse prominence decreasing from middle-age onwards. These changes correlate with remaining lifespan and likely reflect reduced NPC transport capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 establish Msn2 as a frequency-modulated transcription factor (C84-C86, supported by citations) and demonstrate age-related changes in pulse dynamics (C87-C88) with statistical correlations to lifespan (C89). The interpretation that this reflects NPC function (C90-C91) is reasonable given that Msn2 dynamics depend on import/export rates (C86), though C91 is appropriately qualified as speculative. The experimental approach is sophisticated and well-controlled.

results.result: The authors propose a model where compromised NPC assembly and quality control lead to accumulation of misassembled NPCs that are covered with membrane, resulting in fewer functional NPCs and reduced transport dynamics without creating leaky pores.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 integrate multiple lines of evidence into a coherent model: decreased FG-Nups (C93), absence of leaky NPCs (C95), presence of membrane-covered structures (C96), and reduced transport (C97). The model is consistent with all experimental observations and supported by EM data (Figure 3) and prior literature on membrane-covered misassembled NPCs (C96). While the model is inferential, it is the most parsimonious explanation for the data.

results.result: NPC defects in aging may be a consequence of imbalanced protein levels of NPC components and assembly factors, driven by posttranscriptional mechanisms related to protein synthesis, folding, and assembly rather than transcriptional changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 integrate the current findings with prior work (Janssens et al., 2015) showing protein biogenesis imbalance as a driver of aging. The posttranscriptional nature is well-supported by stable transcripts (C101) despite protein changes. The network analysis placing Nups in middle clusters (C103) supports their role as both consequences and drivers of aging. The correlations with lifespan (C104) provide additional support for causal relationships.

results.result: The cellular abundance and localization of nuclear transport receptors (Crm1, Kap60, Kap95) remain relatively stable during aging.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by proteomics data (Janssens et al., 2015) and imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. This is an important control showing that changes in transport are not due to altered NTR levels. The data are straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: This work provides the first clear example that assembly of large protein complexes is a major challenge in aging of dividing cells, with implications for other complexes like the proteasome and kinetochores.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 asserts novelty ('first clear example') which is difficult to verify without comprehensive literature review. C109 is supported by citations showing loss of stoichiometry is conserved. C110 is explicitly speculative about other complexes. While the work on NPCs is well-supported, the broader claim about being 'first' and the speculation about other complexes make this result uncertain in scope. The NPC-specific findings are solid, but the generalization requires additional validation.

results.result: Background information establishing the fundamental properties of NPCs, nuclear transport, and yeast replicative aging as a model system.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C12-C24 provide established background knowledge about NPCs, nuclear transport, and yeast aging, all supported by appropriate citations to review articles and primary literature. These are well-established facts in the field and serve as context for the experimental work. No novel findings are claimed in these statements.

results.result: There is significant cell-to-cell variation in both lifespan and protein levels among individual yeast cells, with some Nups (like Nup2) showing high variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37, C39 document biological variability in single-cell measurements, supported by multiple prior studies (C36) and the current imaging data (C37, C39). This is an important observation for interpreting the correlation analyses but is not a primary finding. The variability is well-documented in the heatmaps and appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Background information on NPC maintenance, oxidative damage, misassembled NPCs in mutants, and quality control mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45, C51-C52, C58, C60-C61 provide background from prior literature about NPC biology, all supported by appropriate citations. These establish the context for testing oxidative damage and assembly defects in aging. No novel findings are claimed; these are established facts used to motivate the experimental approaches.

results.result: Mechanistic explanation for why reduced NPC numbers would affect compartmentalization and comparison with prior conflicting results from Lord et al.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 provides a mechanistic explanation for the compartmentalization phenotype based on rate-limiting steps in transport, supported by multiple citations. C80 acknowledges a discrepancy with prior work and suggests experimental differences as explanation. The mechanistic reasoning is sound and the acknowledgment of conflicting data is appropriate, though the explanation for the discrepancy is speculative.

results.result: Speculation about broader consequences of NPC decline for protein homeostasis, genome stability, and age-related disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 are explicitly speculative about consequences of NPC decline beyond what was directly measured. C105 and C106 are logical inferences but lack direct experimental support in this study. C107 is a broader conclusion about NPC importance in aging, supported by the current findings and a citation (Fichtman and Harel, 2014), but represents interpretation rather than direct demonstration. These are reasonable speculations for the Discussion but not experimentally validated results.
